Smart India Hackathon 2026 · Team Armageddon

GodsEye

A city-wide ANPR platform for Kolkata. It reads number plates off traffic cameras, reconstructs where any vehicle has been all day, and turns the same stream of reads into live traffic analytics.

  • 35camera sites
  • 5,556plate reads
  • 420vehicles tracked
  • 18msper plate

Tracking

Type a plate, get the whole day

Search WB 22 AX 0877 — a vehicle on the watchlist as stolen — and the platform reconstructs its journey: 18 sightings across 13 cameras, 114 km, drawn along the roads it must have taken rather than straight lines between dots.

Search is confusion-aware: type WB22A×0877 with a character the camera misread and it still finds the vehicle, because the distance it ranks by charges less for the substitutions this reader is known to make.

The hard part

The cameras are on poles

An Indian enforcement camera sits five to eight metres up, looking down at the carriageway. That one fact decides everything: the plate is foreshortened, 40–260 pixels wide, JPEG-compressed at that size, then cropped and digitally zoomed — so the artefacts get magnified along with the characters.

So the training images come from a physical camera model, not filters over a clean render: pole height and lens angle, then fog, rain streaks and lens droplets, then headlight glare and exposure, then motion blur, then sensor noise, then the encoder, then the operator's zoom — in the order the physics actually happens.

What the realism cost, and bought

The honest number moved twice

The first version of this project scored 87% — against its own weak filters. Against camera-realistic captures the same engine scored 12%. That gap is the finding: the augmentation had been inflating the headline number sevenfold, and hiding which part of the design was wrong.

What was wrong was the recogniser. It cut the plate into characters and classified each one, and after a JPEG encoder has worked on a 90-pixel plate the gaps between characters simply are not in the image any more. Replacing it with a network that never cuts — a CRNN reading the whole plate at once — doubled accuracy and made it seven times faster.

CaptureCut & classifyCRNN
Daylight53%74%
Night, infrared48%81%
Monsoon rain27%58%
Fog14%37%
Motion blur3%25%
Per read124 ms18 ms

Analytics & alerts

The same reads, aggregated

Two sightings of one plate at two cameras give a distance and a time — so a speed, so congestion. Aggregated over every vehicle, that is the city: heat that follows the roads, origin–destination demand, and bottlenecks ranked by vehicle-minutes of delay caused rather than by slowness, because a slow empty road is not a problem.

Straight about it

What it does not do

It refuses about a third of captures. Anything the reader cannot stand behind is dropped rather than stored, so trajectories have gaps an operator has to bridge. For a system that puts a registration in front of a police officer, refusing to answer is the correct answer — a wrong plate is worse than no plate.

The cameras are simulated and the plates are synthetic — this is measured against a stated camera model, not a field trial. The reader is a number-plate reader: it decodes an Indian registration and deliberately declines handwriting, signage and arbitrary text, which is exactly what buys the accuracy above.

Running it

Three commands

pip install -r requirements.txt
python seed.py                             # a day of city traffic
uvicorn api.main:app --port 8000           # API + live feed
streamlit run dashboard/app.py             # the control room

Python, OpenCV, PyTorch (CPU), FastAPI, Streamlit and deck.gl. No GPU, no internet, no dataset download — the corpus is generated. Without PyTorch it falls back to the classical reader and still runs.
